titre: Claudette Colvin, the Teenager Erased Before Rosa Parks (1955)
accroche: On March 2, 1955, a 15-year-old girl refuses to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus: nine months before Rosa Parks.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 2, 1955, in Montgomery, a 15-year-old girl is riding the bus home from school. The driver, Robert W. Cleere, orders her, along with three other Black passengers, to give up her seat to a white passenger. The other three get up; Claudette Colvin stays seated, next to a pregnant woman, Ruth Hamilton. Two police officers, Thomas J. Ward and Paul Headley, drag her backward off the bus, handcuff her, and one of them hits her in the process. She is charged with disorderly conduct, violating segregation laws, and assaulting an officer, and is sentenced by the juvenile court to a $10 fine. Nine months later, on December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks refuses to do the same thing on the same kind of bus, and becomes the face of the boycott that follows. Colvin, for her part, vanishes from the story for decades.

## A Strategic Choice, Not an Accident

The Montgomery civil rights movement did not turn Colvin's arrest into a public cause: it is now widely accepted that her young age and her pregnancy out of wedlock, which followed in the months after, weighed into that choice, including in the eyes of part of the Black community itself, more cautious on this point. When the boycott begins, on December 5, 1955, it is Rosa Parks who becomes its face: secretary of the local NAACP chapter, married since 1932 and employed as a seamstress, she offered an image the white press could not as easily turn against the cause.

## The Case That Really Ended Segregation

What history rarely remembers is that Parks's act did not, on its own, bring down the law: the lawyer Clifford Durr feared that her criminal case, on appeal, would get bogged down in the state courts. It was another suit, filed on February 1, 1956, in federal court, *Browder v. Gayle*, that directly challenged the constitutionality of segregation on Montgomery's buses. Its four plaintiffs were Aurelia Browder, Susie McDonald, Mary Louise Smith, and Claudette Colvin. On June 5, 1956, a three-judge panel ruled, two votes to one, that this segregation violated the Fourteenth Amendment of the Constitution; the Supreme Court affirmed the ruling on November 13, and the order took effect on December 20, 1956. The figure who carried the boycott to public opinion and the legal instrument that ended segregation are therefore not the same person: Colvin, pushed off the public stage because she was judged too inconvenient, nonetheless remains one of the four names on the decision that actually changed the law.

repere.texte: Twenty months pass between Colvin's arrest, on March 2, 1955, and the Supreme Court's affirmation of the ruling, on November 13, 1956, and it is her name, along with three others, that appears on the decision that legally ends segregation on Montgomery's buses, not that of Rosa Parks.

carte.punch: Before Rosa Parks, a 15-year-old girl did the same thing, and the movement set her aside.
carte.idee: On March 2, 1955, Claudette Colvin, 15, refuses to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, nine months before Rosa Parks. Judged too young and pregnant out of wedlock to embody the boycott, she is set aside, but remains one of the four plaintiffs in the federal lawsuit that ends segregation in 1956.

quiz.question: Why did the civil rights leaders not make Claudette Colvin the face of the boycott?
choix: Because she already had a stable job at the NAACP
Because her trial had ended in a dismissal
Because she had refused to file a complaint against the driver
Because her young age and her pregnancy would have exposed her to a hostile press
quiz.explication: Colvin was a minor and pregnant out of wedlock; the leaders preferred Rosa Parks, the married and employed NAACP secretary, judged less vulnerable to a hostile press campaign: the other three options are invented.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which federal ruling legally ends segregation on Montgomery's buses, and what is its connection to Claudette Colvin?
choix: Rosa Parks's trial, in which her original conviction is overturned on appeal
*Browder v. Gayle*, in which Colvin is one of the four plaintiffs
*Plessy v. Ferguson*, reopened in 1956 at the request of the NAACP
A presidential order signed by Eisenhower in response to the boycott
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Filed on February 1, 1956, in federal court, *Browder v. Gayle* counted Claudette Colvin among its four plaintiffs, and its ruling ended segregation on the buses.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is the pregnant passenger seated next to Claudette Colvin at the time of her arrest?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Claudette Colvin stayed seated near a pregnant woman, Ruth Hamilton, when police officers Thomas Ward and Paul Headley forced her off the bus.
